title: Write a `Supplier<Employee>` that creates a default employee.
shortTitle: Write a Supplier<Employee> that creates a default employee

s1_definition.profdef: `Supplier<T>` is a functional interface with a single `get()` method that takes no input and returns a value. A `Supplier<Employee>` lazily produces an Employee each time `get()` is called, commonly used to supply defaults or deferred values.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Supplier<T>` is a functional interface with a single `get()` method that takes no input and returns a value. A `Supplier<Employee>` lazily produces an Employee each time `get()` is called, commonly used to supply defaults or deferred values.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya keeps a stamp that prints a blank default employee form on demand. Whenever she needs one, she presses the stamp — no inputs needed, out comes a fresh default.

**One line to remember:** `Supplier<Employee>` takes nothing and returns a fresh Employee from `get()` — perfect for lazy defaults.

sections.s2_technical:
A Supplier has no arguments and returns a value, so `Supplier<Employee> defaultEmployee = () -> new Employee("UNKNOWN", 0)` creates a default each time get is called. Because it is lazy, the object is built only when needed — this is why Optional's `orElseGet(supplier)` takes a Supplier rather than a value: the default is constructed only if the Optional is empty.

This laziness distinguishes `orElseGet(() -> expensiveDefault())` from `orElse(expensiveDefault())`, where orElse always builds the default even when it is not used. A Supplier is also how you pass a factory without invoking it, for example `Stream.generate(defaultEmployee)` to produce a stream of defaults.

The senior nuance is using Supplier to defer expensive or side-effecting construction and to avoid building objects that may be discarded. In logging I use supplier-form messages so the string is assembled only if the level is enabled. Choosing a Supplier over a precomputed value is a laziness and performance decision — you pay the construction cost only when the value is actually consumed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A lookup at the National Bank of India returns an Optional employee, and when it is empty the caller needs a default placeholder employee, but building the default should happen only when needed.

This is exactly what a Supplier does — orElseGet with a Supplier builds the default employee lazily, only when the lookup found nothing.

The code defines an `EmployeeLookupService` using a Supplier default and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: lookups for Rajesh (present) and Nobody (absent).

Step 1: For Rajesh, the map returns the real employee, so the Optional is non-empty.

Step 2: orElseGet sees a value present and returns it without ever calling the Supplier, so no default is built.

Step 3: For Nobody, the Optional is empty, so orElseGet invokes the Supplier.

Step 4: The Supplier builds the UNKNOWN default employee, returned to the caller.

```
INFO: found   = Rajesh
INFO: missing = UNKNOWN
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  findOrDefault("Rajesh") → Optional[Rajesh] → orElseGet → Rajesh (supplier NOT called)
  findOrDefault("Nobody") → Optional.empty   → orElseGet → supplier.get() → UNKNOWN
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Lazy Default via Supplier ═══

  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ ──Employee──→ caller
  │ name     │→│ EmployeeLookupService│
  │          │ │ orElseGet(supplier)  │
  └──────────┘ └──────────────────────┘
     default built only when lookup is empty
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Supplier<T> ═══

  ┌─ laziness ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Supplier<T> get(): T — no input, returns a value           │
  │ orElseGet(supplier): builds default ONLY if empty (lazy)   │
  │ orElse(value): ALWAYS builds the value (eager) — wasteful  │
  │ Stream.generate(supplier) → infinite stream of values      │
  │ log.info(() -> msg): assemble string only if level enabled │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │      EmployeeLookupService    │
  │  - defaultEmployee: Supplier   │ () -> new Employee(...)
  │  + findOrDefault(String): Emp  │ orElseGet(defaultEmployee)
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. Optional.ofNullable(db.get(name))
  2. orElseGet(defaultEmployee)
  3. supplier.get() only if empty
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Supplier is a functional interface with a single get method that takes no input and returns a value, so a Supplier of Employee lazily produces an Employee each time it is called. I use it to provide a default placeholder employee, for example a lambda returning a new UNKNOWN employee, and I plug it into Optional's orElseGet so that the default is constructed only when the lookup actually came back empty.

That laziness is the whole point and it is why I prefer orElseGet with a Supplier over orElse with a precomputed value. orElse always builds its default even when the Optional has a value and the default is thrown away, whereas orElseGet calls the Supplier only in the empty case. On a lookup at the National Bank of India that matters whenever constructing the default is expensive or has side-effects.

The senior point I add is that a Supplier lets me pass a factory without invoking it — I can feed it to Stream dot generate to produce a stream of values, or use the supplier form of logging so the message string is assembled only when the log level is enabled. Choosing a Supplier over a ready-made value is a deliberate laziness and performance decision: I pay the construction cost only when the value is genuinely consumed.
